title: Don't take the tool's own claim at face value
explanation: `brokerctl start` refuses and says a WAL reservation is present, "assuming another instance is still using it" — but that's an assumption stated in the error message, not a verified fact. `pgrep -af eventqueue-worker` returning nothing proves no broker process actually exists anywhere on the box, so whatever is blocking the start isn't a live conflict.

title: Recognize why a presence-based check can lie
explanation: `brokerctl` treats the mere existence of `wal.reserved` plus low free space as evidence of a live claim — a reasonable check while a broker is genuinely running, but one that can't distinguish an active reservation from a stale leftover. The box lost power mid-run last night, so the process that wrote the reservation never got the chance to remove it on exit; the file outlived the thing it was supposed to represent.

title: Confirm what's actually consuming the space
explanation: `ls -lh /var/lib/eventqueue` shows a single ~13MB `wal.reserved` file eating nearly the entire bounded tmpfs — a fixed-size pre-reservation eventqueue's start logic writes up front specifically so a write-ahead-log write never has to fail partway through mid-write.

title: Remove it, since nothing is holding it
explanation: `sudo rm /var/lib/eventqueue/wal.reserved` is safe precisely because step 1 already established no process references it. Deleting a reservation file that's still actively backing a running broker would be dangerous; deleting a confirmed-orphaned one just returns unused space.

title: Restart and verify against both symptoms
explanation: `brokerctl start` now succeeds — it claims a fresh reservation for itself and launches. Checking both `pgrep -af eventqueue-worker` (process actually running) and `df -h /var/lib/eventqueue` (healthy free space) matters because either one alone could look fine while the other is still broken.

title: The durable version of this fix isn't a file check at all
explanation: A file's existence can never tell you, on its own, whether the thing that created it is still alive — that's true of any lock/reservation file, not just this one. The robust pattern is a liveness check the OS enforces automatically, like an `flock` held for the holder's entire lifetime: the kernel releases it the instant the holding process dies, crash or no crash, so there's nothing stale left to misinterpret.
